cards.title: Phonological Similarity Effect
cards.aim: Show that people recode silently read items into a speech-based form.
cards.manipulated: Lists of letters that sound alike versus sound different. On some trials people also said 'one, two, three, four' out loud (articulatory suppression) and on others stayed quiet.
cards.measured: How well people clicked the letters back in the order shown.
cards.found: Sound-alike lists were recalled worse, even when read silently. With suppression on visual lists, the cost disappeared.
cards.means: People turn what they see into a sound code, which supports the phonological loop.
cards.trap: It is about similar sound, not similar look (E and F would be a visual mix-up).

cards.title: Neighborhood Size Effect
cards.aim: Test whether long-term knowledge of words affects short-term recall.
cards.manipulated: Words from large neighborhoods (like cat) versus small neighborhoods (like hippopotamus).
cards.measured: How well people recalled the words in order.
cards.found: Large neighborhood words were recalled better in short-term memory tasks.
cards.means: What you know in long-term memory helps short-term recall, so memory span is not a pure measure of short-term capacity.
cards.trap: A neighbor differs by one letter or one sound; do not confuse it with a word that merely means the same thing.

cards.title: Brown-Peterson Task
cards.aim: Find out what happens to short-term memory when rehearsal is blocked.
cards.manipulated: How long people did a distractor task (counting backwards) before recall.
cards.measured: How well people recalled the consonants.
cards.found: The longer the distraction, the worse the recall.
cards.means: The researchers concluded short-term memory loses information through decay unless it is rehearsed.
cards.trap: Decay is the researchers' conclusion, and interference (Keppel and Underwood, 1962) was cited as an alternative.

cards.title: Modality Effect
cards.aim: Test whether hearing a list gives better memory than reading it.
cards.manipulated: Lists that were heard versus read silently (digits in random order).
cards.measured: Memory for the last one or two items.
cards.found: Heard lists gave better memory for the last items. Lip-read or mouthed lists show it too.
cards.means: Hearing adds information about how the list sounded (Neath and Surprenant, 2003), and the effect shaped ideas about sensory memory.
cards.trap: The effect is for the last items of the list, not the whole list.

cards.title: Partial Report
cards.aim: Test whether the small amount people report from a brief display is a recall limit or a perception limit.
cards.manipulated: Whether a cue telling which part to report came right away or after a delay.
cards.measured: How much of the cued part people reported.
cards.found: With an immediate cue, people reported the cued part almost perfectly. With a delayed cue, performance fell toward the usual limit.
cards.means: A sensory (iconic) store briefly held nearly all the display, and it fades very fast. The limit is reporting time, not perception.
cards.trap: The limit is in recall, not in what people saw.

cards.title: Position Error Effect
cards.aim: Show how order errors in recall are patterned.
cards.manipulated: Nothing was compared across groups. Each recalled letter's placed position was compared with its true position.
cards.measured: Where each recalled item was placed in the list.
cards.found: Items were usually placed correctly. Errors were systematic: the item landed in an adjacent position.
cards.means: People keep approximate position information, and percent correct alone hides this.

cards.title: Mental Rotation
cards.aim: Test whether mental images behave like real images.
cards.manipulated: How much one block shape was turned relative to the other (same shape or mirror image).
cards.measured: How long people took to judge same or mirror image.
cards.found: The larger the turn, the longer the response, at a constant rate.
cards.means: People mentally rotate images, so mental images are much like real images.
cards.trap: Self-reports of imagery are unreliable, so researchers use tasks that require imagery.

cards.title: Typical Reasoning
cards.researcher: Tversky and Kahneman (1983); Shafir, Smith, and Osherson (1990)
cards.aim: Show that people judge probability with heuristics.
cards.manipulated: People rated how likely descriptions of a person were to fit single professions or activities versus combinations.
cards.measured: Ratings of how likely each statement was.
cards.found: People sometimes rated a combination as more likely than one of its parts (conjunction fallacy).
cards.means: People use heuristics, not the rules of probability.
cards.trap: A combination can never be more likely than either part alone.

cards.title: Wason Selection
cards.aim: Compare how well people test abstract rules and familiar thematic rules.
cards.manipulated: Abstract rules (letters and numbers) versus thematic rules (like borrowing a car).
cards.measured: Which cards people chose to turn over.
cards.found: Thematic rules were much easier. On the abstract rule most people chose D and 3 instead of D and 7.
cards.means: With relevant experience people test rules well; with abstract rules they must use logic alone.
cards.trap: The 3 can only confirm the rule; the 7 could falsify it.

cards.title: Decision Making
cards.researcher: Kahneman and Tversky (1982); Tversky and Kahneman
cards.aim: Show that wording or context can change choices between equivalent options.
cards.manipulated: The same choice framed with gain wording versus loss wording.
cards.found: Gain wording led to the sure option and loss wording to the gamble.
cards.means: Choices can follow the framing and not the substance.

cards.title: Monty Hall
cards.aim: Show poor intuition about the probability of combined events.
cards.manipulated: Whether people stayed with their first door or switched after the host opened a no-prize door.
cards.measured: How often staying and switching won.
cards.found: Switching wins about two-thirds of the time and staying about one-third. Many people think it makes no difference.
cards.means: The first pick stays at 1 in 3, so the other 2 in 3 moves to the remaining door.
cards.trap: The two remaining doors are not equally likely.

cards.title: Risky Decisions
cards.aim: Show that risky choices depend on whether outcomes are seen as gains or losses.
cards.manipulated: Whether the sure outcome was a gain or a loss, with a gamble as the alternative.
cards.measured: Whether people took the sure thing or the gamble.
cards.found: People avoided risk with gains (sure thing) and sought risk with losses (gamble).
cards.means: Risk decisions depend on how outcomes are perceived, not only on objective odds.
cards.trap: Losses lead to gambling, not caution.

cards.title: German & Defeyter (2000): Immunity to functional fixedness in young children
cards.aim: Test whether young children get stuck on an object's usual function (functional fixedness).
cards.manipulated: Whether the box had first been shown as a container (preutilization) or not, in 5-, 6- and 7-year-olds.
cards.measured: How long children took to offer the box as a support.
cards.found: Children aged 6 and 7 were slower after seeing the box as a container. 5-year-olds were not slowed and were even faster than the older children after seeing the box as a container.
cards.means: Younger children have a more fluid idea of function, so one shown use did not lock the object in.
cards.trap: Younger children did better here, not worse.

cards.title: Leist et al. (2022): Irrelevant speech impairs serial recall of verbal but not spatial items
cards.aim: Find out whether ignored speech hurts only verbal items or spatial items too.
cards.manipulated: Verbal versus spatial items; quiet, steady-state or changing-state speech to ignore; third graders versus adults.
cards.measured: Serial recall of the order of the items.
cards.found: Speech hurt verbal recall but not spatial recall, in children and adults.
cards.means: The effect is specific to verbal material, which fits phonological interference better than attention capture or changing-state accounts.
cards.trap: Changing-state speech hurts more than steady-state, but only for verbal items.

cards.title: Morrison & Richmond (2020): Offloading items from memory
cards.aim: Find out who offloads items from memory and whether it helps.
cards.manipulated: A no-choice block (memory only) versus a choice block where pen and paper were allowed, with lists of different lengths.
cards.measured: Recall and how much people wrote things down.
cards.found: Offloading improved memory, especially at high loads, and people offloaded more as load grew.
cards.means: Memory ability did not predict who offloaded, so offloading may be a compensatory strategy across abilities.
cards.trap: Low-capacity people were expected to offload more, but capacity did not predict it.

cards.title: Hoover & Healy (2019): The Bat-and-Ball Problem
cards.aim: Test whether the bat-and-ball error comes from unconsciously ignoring 'more than'.
cards.manipulated: A standard problem with 'more than' versus a control version without it.
cards.measured: Confidence, and later recall and recognition of the problem wording.
cards.found: Wrong reasoners mostly remembered 'more than', so it was not simply overlooked.
cards.means: Substitution cannot be confirmed as the cause, so the authors prefer the term error sensitivity.
cards.trap: The intuitive 10 cents is wrong; the answer is 5 cents.

cards.title: Giuliani et al. (2023): The joint effect of framing and defaults on choice behavior
cards.aim: Test the framing effect and the default effect together.
cards.manipulated: Gain versus loss wording, and no default, a sure default or a risky default, in life-or-death and money scenarios.
cards.measured: Whether people chose the sure or the risky option.
cards.found: A risky default raised risk taking, a sure default did not raise risk aversion, and framing and default effects were additive.
cards.means: People who thought the default was most rational followed it most, though that question came after the choice.
cards.trap: The belief question was exploratory and may be a justification.

cards.title: Chein et al. (2011) and Albert, Chein & Steinberg (2013): Peers and the adolescent brain
cards.researcher: Chein et al. (2011); Albert, Chein and Steinberg (2013)
cards.aim: Explain why adolescents take more risks with peers around.
cards.manipulated: Playing a driving game alone versus watched by friends, in adolescents, young adults and adults.
cards.measured: Risky driving choices and brain activity in reward and cognitive-control regions.
cards.found: Adolescents took more risks when watched, with greater reward-region activity. Cognitive-control regions did not change with peers.
cards.means: The peer effect works mainly through reward circuitry, not weaker reasoning.
cards.trap: Adolescents reason about risk like adults in the lab; the peer context is what changes.
